answers: Chart of accounts, companies (us, customers, suppliers), catalogue items, warehouse locations, VAT rates — each is its own master-data object; companies also store an IBAN where available.

So what we're looking at for master data is this: the chart of accounts gets its own master-data object, the companies we work with — that's ourselves, our customers, and our suppliers — each get their own master-data object, and then the same goes for catalogue items, warehouse locations, and VAT rates, every single one of them a separate master-data object; oh, and for the companies, we also store the bank account number in IBAN format whenever we actually have it.

Each piece of master data — the chart of accounts, the companies we deal with (our own outfit, customers, suppliers), catalogue items, warehouse locations, and VAT rates — lives as its own master-data object, and any company we've got a bank number for also carries that number as an IBAN.

Sales invoices create sales_invoice documents. Fields pulled straight from the invoice: number, issue date, seller and buyer (looked up by NIP), net amount, currency, VAT rate code. VAT = net × rate% ÷ 100, rounded half up to the grosz; gross = net + VAT; due date = issue date + invoice's payment days; status begins as open, can become paid. Open amount starts at gross, drops as payments are matched; partial payment leaves status open. Booking in pl-stat: debit 201 gross, credit 700 net, credit 222 VAT.

So whenever we issue a sales invoice, the system creates a document of type sales_invoice, and it pulls in quite a few fields directly from the invoice itself — the number, the issue date, the seller and the buyer (both identified by NIP), the net amount, the currency, and the VAT rate code. From there, the VAT is calculated as the net amount multiplied by the rate's percentage and then divided by 100, and that result gets rounded half up to the nearest grosz; the gross is simply the net plus that VAT. The due date is worked out by adding the number of payment days printed on the invoice to the issue date. The status field starts out as open and can later be updated to paid. The open amount begins equal to the gross and decreases as payments get matched against the invoice — if it's only partly paid, the status stays open. In the ledger book pl-stat, each one of these invoices gets posted with a debit to account 201 for the gross, a credit to account 700 for the net, and a credit to account 222 for the VAT.

Every invoice we send out gets logged as a sales_invoice — grabs the number, issue date, seller and buyer by NIP, net amount, currency, and VAT rate code right off the invoice. VAT's calculated as net times the rate percent over 100, half-up rounded to the grosz, gross is just net plus that VAT, and the due date is whatever the issue date is plus however many payment days are on the invoice. Kicks off with status open, flips to paid later on. Open amount starts at the gross and ticks down as payments come in and get matched; still open if it's only partly paid. Hits pl-stat as: debit 201 for the gross, credit 700 for the net, credit 222 for the VAT.

Each delivery produces exactly one PZ document — type pz — carrying the supplier, the supplier's delivery document number, the warehouse location, the date, and the currency. Every item on that delivery becomes a pz_line tied to that PZ, holding qty, price, and value, where value equals qty multiplied by the unit price from the delivery. Each pz_line moves the item's stock into the delivery's location and posts to book pl-stat: debit 330, credit 300, at that line's value.

So for every single delivery that comes in, we create one document — we're calling the type pz, so it's a PZ document — and on that document we record the supplier, the supplier's delivery document number, the warehouse location, the date, and the currency, all of it. Then every item that was actually delivered gets its own line on that PZ, and that line type is called pz_line, and it points back to the PZ it belongs to. Each pz_line has three fields: qty, price, and value, and that value is just qty times the unit price as it appears on the delivery. Now, every one of those lines does two things: it pushes that item's stock into whatever location the delivery was for, and it makes a posting in the book pl-stat — debit goes to account 330, credit goes to account 300 — and the amount posted is the line's value.

One delivery, one PZ — that's the type name, pz — with the supplier, their delivery doc number, the warehouse location, the date, the currency, done. Every delivered item gets a pz_line hanging off that PZ: fields are qty, price, value, and value is just qty times the unit price on the delivery. That line shoves the stock into the delivery's location and hits book pl-stat for that value — 330 debit, 300 credit.

A supplier's invoice maps to a purchase_invoice document with these fields: number, invoice_date, supplier (looked up by NIP), owner (our company), net amount, currency, and VAT rate code. VAT = net × rate_percent / 100, rounded half up to the grosz; gross = net + VAT. Status begins as open and shifts to paid once fully settled. The open amount starts at gross and decreases as payments are matched; partial payment leaves the status open. Booking goes to pl-stat: debit 300 for net, debit 221 for VAT, credit 202 for gross.

So when a supplier sends us an invoice, what we do is create a document of type purchase_invoice, and on that document we record the number, the invoice date, and we find the supplier using their NIP, and then our own company goes in as the owner field, and after that we put in the net amount, the currency, and the VAT rate code. Now, to work out the VAT, you take the net, multiply it by whatever percent that rate code carries, divide by 100, and then you round it half up to the nearest grosz, and the gross is just that VAT added on top of the net. The status field kicks off as open, and it only moves over to paid once everything has been matched. The open amount is set to the gross right at the start and it ticks down every time a payment gets matched against it, but if it's only partly paid it just sits there still showing open. For the actual bookkeeping entry in pl-stat, you debit account 300 with the net, debit account 221 with the VAT, and credit account 202 with the gross.

Supplier invoice comes in, we slap it into the system as a purchase_invoice — number, invoice date, supplier pulled by NIP, our company as owner, net amount, currency, VAT rate code, the whole lot. VAT's just net times the rate's percent over 100, half-up rounding to the grosz, then gross is net plus that VAT. Status kicks off at open, flips to paid when it's fully matched. Open amount starts at gross, drops as payments hit it — partly paid still stays open. pl-stat gets the posting: 300 debited for net, 221 debited for VAT, 202 credited for gross.
Each warehouse release creates a goods_issue document—fields: item, location, quantity, date, reason—and cuts that item's stock from its location.

So when you pull something out of the warehouse, what happens is the system generates a goods issue document, and this document is of the type goods_issue, carrying four fields plus one more: item, location, quantity, date, and reason — and every single one of those issue transactions actually reduces that particular item's stock level at its location.
Pulling stuff out of the warehouse? That makes a goods_issue doc — item, location, quantity, date, reason — and each one knocks that item's stock out of its location.

Each line on a bank statement generates a bank_line record carrying date, amount, currency, direction, the title as reference, the counterparty and its account, and our account; open amount is initialised to the full amount, status starts as open and flips to settled once nothing remains open. Incoming money is applied to the customer's open sales invoices in this sequence: the invoice named in the title; that same invoice when the payment is within 0.02 short or over, with the gap written off to account 755; an invoice matching the exact amount; the smallest group of invoices summing to it, capped at 4; a partial payment against the named invoice; otherwise the oldest open invoices in turn until the money runs out. Outgoing money follows the identical sequence against the supplier's open purchase invoices for the account the money goes to, except there is no tolerance. A match reduces the open amounts on both the invoices and the bank line by whatever was allocated, marking each as paid or settled when nothing remains open, and writes one settlement record per invoice containing the payment, the document type and id, the amount, and the date. A difference that falls within the tolerance becomes a matching difference record holding kind, amount, currency, direction, account, and date; if that difference is short, it is also posted in book pl-stat as a debit to the difference account and a credit to 201.

So basically every single line you pull off a bank statement turns into its own bank_line record — you've got date, amount, currency, direction, the title sitting there as the reference, the counterparty plus their account, and then our account too; the open amount kicks off equal to the full amount, status is open right away and only switches over to settled once absolutely nothing is left open. When money comes in you're trying to match it against that customer's open sales invoices, and you work through the options in a specific order: first you look for the exact invoice the title mentions; then you check whether that same invoice is within 0.02 — either short or over — and if so you write the gap off to 755; after that you hunt for any invoice that's the exact same amount; then you try to find the fewest invoices that add up to it, but you stop at 4 invoices maximum; next you'd do a partial hit on the named invoice; and if none of that works you just go oldest-first through the open invoices until the cash runs out. Money going out runs through the exact same steps but against the supplier's open purchase invoices for whichever account the money is heading to, and there's no tolerance rule there. Whenever a match lands, you knock the open amounts down on both the invoices and the bank line by what got allocated — calling it paid or settled when nothing's left open — and you log a settlement record for each invoice that includes the payment, the document type and id, the amount, and the date. Any difference that's within the tolerance gets its own matching difference record with kind, amount, currency, direction, account, and date on it, and when that difference is on the short side you also book it in pl-stat, debiting the difference account and crediting 201.

Bank statement line → bank_line record: date, amount, currency, direction, title as reference, counterparty and counterparty account, our account; open amount equals amount; status is open, becomes settled when open amount hits zero. Inbound cash matches the paying customer's open sales invoices in order: invoice named in title; that invoice ±0.02, gap to 755; invoice of identical amount; fewest invoices totalling that amount, max 4; partial on the named invoice; oldest open invoices until funds are exhausted. Outbound cash matches identically against the receiving supplier's open purchase invoices, no tolerance applied. Each match reduces invoice open amounts and bank line open amount by the allocated figure, sets status to paid or settled when cleared, and produces one settlement record per invoice: payment, document type and id, amount, date. A within-tolerance difference produces a matching difference record: kind, amount, currency, direction, account, date; a short difference is additionally posted in pl-stat — debit the difference account, credit 201.

Complaints get logged as complaint docs with a number, customer, and details. Each one automatically spawns a case-type record whose subject is that complaint number, starting at open status and moveable to resolved.

So when a complaint comes in, you create a complaint document — it needs a number, the customer, and the details of the complaint. That complaint document then opens up a follow-up record, and this record is of a type called case. The subject of that case is set to the complaint number, and when it's first created its status is open, though later on you can move that status over to resolved.

Every complaint gets its own complaint doc — number, customer, details — and that kicks off a follow-up using a type called case, with the complaint number as the subject, status kicking off at open and able to flip to resolved down the line.
A withdrawn complaint gets its case marked as resolved.
So basically what happens is, when a customer goes ahead and withdraws their complaint, the case tied to that complaint ends up being resolved — that's how it works.
Customer pulls the complaint, case goes to resolved.

A stock count for an item at a location creates a stock_level record with four fields: date, counted, book, and difference. Date is the count date, counted is the counted quantity, book is the item's stock movements into the location minus those out of it up to and including the count date, and difference is counted minus book.

So when you do a stock count for an item at a location, what you're recording is a new type called stock_level, and it's got these four fields on it — date, counted, book, and difference — where date is the count date, counted is how many you counted, book is basically all the stock movements into that location for that item minus all the movements out of it dated up to and including the count date, and then difference is just counted minus book.

Each stock count of an item at a location lays down a stock_level — that's the type name — carrying the fields date, counted, book, and difference: date holds the count date, counted holds the counted quantity, book is the total of that item's inbound stock movements at the location minus the outbound ones dated up to and including the count date, and difference is counted minus book.
